As for me (don’t hold this against me) I was a financial planner, now retired. I loved my career because it fostered and placed me in an environment to continue learning about money, investing my learnings and helping others on their own journey to realise their ideal lives, underpinned with achieving financial independence.

Anyways I wont bore you with my journey, aside to say we rented our home in a big city (Sydney), then relocated to a costal regional town in Australia (Cairns). Where we continued to expand and grow our business, without financial pressure i.e. engaging with only those we that were also aligned to our values and were happy to engage our services. Last year we sold our business for a premium, I’d say because we’d built a right kind of business and now we’re retired at 52yo.

I truly believe the world is our oyster and I love to travel.

I also love Japan, their seasons, nature, cuisine, history, and culture. So much so that I bought an apartment here and renovated it for less than $100k USD. Actually I’m here now writing this before I head into town on a free shuttle bus after which I’m going skiing ($250 USD for a season pass).

Today my FIRE life consists of travelling between Cairns & Niigata 10 months of the year and the remaining 2 months somewhere else in the world.

The cost? Holding cost of Cairns & Niigata apartments are total approx $10k USD pa. Another $5k USD for travel/flights/shinkansen etc, $15k USD pa more for day to day living expenses and another $10k USD pa for fun (Fat FIRE).

My point is and hopefully it also inspires others I’m living comfortably on $40k USD pa, living in two countries, and travelling to other countries too (in March I’m heading to Malaysia, Thailand and Philippines for 8 weeks), this tick all my boxes (nature, beaches, mountains, intellectual stimulation, cuisine, friendships and new adventures).

Can I afford to be spending more on my current lifestyle? Heck yes. This current lifestyle spending is actually less than 20% pa of my annual investment income. So why didn’t I do all this earlier?

As to high incomes, yes our clients valued our services and paid us well, however in truth money was/has never been never been my main driver, it was just the result of putting others (our clients) first. So whilst I could have retired at 45yo, I kept going because, heck why not, when you love helping others, they’re happy to pay you, and you have great relationships, this is small business nirvana.

On a final note, YES YOU CAN relocate even when you are building your career or business, but only do so as long as the relocation helps develop and support your core values and you to express your authentic self; and it is a destination or milestone on your journey to financial independence and aligned to you living your ideal life.

Just like water stagnating becomes septic over along period of staying still, changing ones environment is not only healthy but at times essential for ones very survival.

Ok enough dribbling here hahaha, clouds are clearing, think I will go skiing now :) Keep up the great posts! Peter

Very cool! Sounds like you are living the dream

I haven’t seen many articles address clearly an apples to apples look at how affordable housing is compared to 40+ years ago. I always find it interesting when younger individuals such as myself complain that they will never be able to afford a house like their parents. But so many factors have changed. First being the demands that people have for their housing. Compared to generations before houses are huge, their trim levels are way higher, granite/quartz used to be a luxury but now it’s almost like the same people think it’s a right. You can have a nice house, that serves a very utilitarian purpose, is energy efficient and in a good neighborhood in many areas, as you have illustrated. But watching a show on HGTV like House Hunters where everyone has unrealistic wants and demands, for a standard house that has evolved into a modern day reflection of our social media driven, American consumerism, they will never be able to afford that. Way to many people blowing way to much of their salary and still expecting to buy a house with way more features and luxuries than generations before will definitely make it unaffordable.. I am not sure why that is not more obvious.. but I guess hedonic adaption is expanding exponentially from generation to generation in the US.

The question is this “Are the hom with less luxuries avaliable to buy?” or does an investor see that home, install the features and luxieries and then sell or rent it.

There’s a lot of truth to the reality that people want larger and larger houses these days. But I think at least part of it, once again, goes back to ZONING LAWS! Cute little 2BR and 3BR single family houses can’t be built due to zoning laws or economically not viable to build these days. This is a serious problem. Something’s gotta give.

I am far beyond the point of having to move because of economic reasons, but my children definitely had to face the reality of astronomical house price appreciation in the Greater Toronto Area. I advised them to “get outta Dodge” if at all possible, and build a life beyond the familiarity of the city they grew up in. Fortunately for them (and happily for me – not because they are away from me, but because it’s economically and financially advantageous for them), they all moved away. One of them was fortunate enough to find employment in the U.S., so he’s making almost double the income that he would have in Canada (in the field of medicine), even though the city he’s in is quite expensive. It’s also far more exciting for young people to live and work in the USA than in boring old Canada. The opportunities and choice of mobility are seemingly endless. So, I agree with MMM – if where you grew up is prohibitively expensive and you’re sticking around just because it’s within your cushy comfort zone, you need to move where houses are significantly less expensive, and figure out how to build a life there. Astronomically expensive housing will choke the life out of you.

Great question, because it’s relevant at any time, and even better answer.

What I’ve appreciated about the Moustachian philosophy (at least from what I can tell) is that it doesn’t assume that we humans deserve to get everything we want and right now!

I’m actually a compulsive debtor in recovery, and reading blogs like this one and books like “Your Money or Your Life,” are very helpful tools for me. My past ridiculous and childish thoughts about money included:

~I deserve this ~Everyone else is doing it, I should be able to as well ~It’s my right ~I shouldn’t have to work and save. I shouldn’t have to sacrifice or make difficult choices.

These thoughts and the silly and financially damaging actions they lead to are not just the affliction of those who are compulsive, but are the foundational philosophy for our consumerist culture.

Just because I live in the U.S., doesn’t mean I deserve to be able to buy a house; especially when I did NOTHING during my pre-recovery days to save for one.

The amazing news is, however, that even though I got into recovery and began to practice sound financial principles only 10 years ago, my hubs and I own a great home in a dream location. We went from overspending each month by about $1,500 (today we’d be almost $250,000 in debt – and that doesn’t include interest payments!) to being worth over $1.5 million (this does include the estimated value of our home).

I work in my dream career and make 2/3 as much money as my hubby, but work 1/4 the time he does (this is the way we both like it).

All this to say that once you turn the ship around, once you begin to change even the smallest behaviors with money to align with Moustachian ideas, it doesn’t take long at all to see HUGE results.

Thanks, Mr. Moustache and all who embrace FIRE and principles of financial sanity! Natalie :^)

I did end up moving and found a whole new and better life!

I had been ‘living’ in San Francisco as a flight attendant in a 3 bedroom with 18 roommates for $375/mo. Since the crew is never there, it wasn’t as uncomfortable but it is the only way that situation worked for the 3 years I did it. I saved a bunch of money and paid off my debts. It also helped socially because our schedules were so wild it was the best way to spend time with people. If I had a bunch of days home I would visit family or friends. My parents were kind enough to store my few items in a spare closet of their house.

I had begun making an excel of places I thought I would like to live and move to then the pandemic hit and it forced me to move as I was laid off. I made a list of requirements including drivable in 2 hours to a major airport/hub or closer if I commuted (I don’t have to go to work every day). It needed to be affordable housing, community-based, good internet (my parents live in Alabama and it’s not available where they live), things for me to do (entertainment), and in a climate with 4 seasons (Alabama has hot or wet, SFO has damp and less damp). I used best places which has a quiz that also asked some other good questions and I decided I probably wanted some kind of university town so there was 24 hour services (because sometimes I work nights) as that would be good for me. I then converted my Honda crv to a van and road tripped and stayed a few days to a week in each area I was considering. When I got to my current town of Harrisonburg Va I fell in love with it. I moved there and bought a house within a few months for $1,100 a month. It needs work since it was built in 1918 but I enjoy that and it has great bones. I put in my transfer to IAD and love it. I later was able to go to a meet up for board gamers which is one of my favorite hobbies. I made a lot of friends and met my husband. Now that I’m back to flying I find I enjoy being home more because I’m not stressed about money since I moved someplace more reasonable and built myself a whole new community for support.

Just move and put yourself out there. Most people are too lazy to make new friends, it takes work and practice but it’s not impossible to make yourself a a new home.

That is so weird. We drove around and spent the night there. It was a great surprise! Virginia really wasn’t on the list., but we were really struck how nice it is.As I mentioned in another post, Fayetteville, Arkansas was also a pleasant surprise. Missouri seemed to have the nicest people. The skid plate under our car was badly damaged when I drove over something and many people stopped and offered to help.

In his book, Paul Terhorst suggested retiring to a State capitol that has a major university,.

I work part time in retail, my wife part time at a library. I found your blog and read every article from beginning to end. We bought a house and have no other debt and currently about 40k invested, not counting our retirement accounts through work, and it started here. I constantly hear comments like the one quoted and continuously have people that make way more than me question how I afford my life. I point them here and know they’re too lazy and married to their excuses they won’t even bother. Everyone loves to complain these days.

I think it’s worth pointing out that “house hacking” does not necessitate breaking your home up into multiple ADUs in the US as you have highlighted through many follower stories on your blog. That being said I hope the broader point you’ve been making since the start of the pandemic will resonate with folks – these swings are long cycles and there are mustachaian activities to participate in even when real estate is off the table. I’m only able to consider moving to the CO area this year after much thumb twiddling in far more affordable Nebraska!

Love this! While I do feel super lucky to have bought my place in Longmont pre-pandemic, after a few years I realized it wasn’t where I wanted to be anymore. I was tired of winter, tired of grind culture, and ready for a big adventure. I spent a year traveling in Latin America, lowkey looking for a new country to live in, and I ended up loving Colombia. Incredible natural beauty, tons to explore, nice people, and an excellent exchange rate. Currently renting a 1BR apartment in a small, safe, outdoorsy city for $260/mo. Hope you’re enjoying winter in AZ, the community you joined sounds awesome!

Thank you Pete. 8 years ago, we decided to relocate from Massachusetts to Tucson, AZ. The transition came with many challenges, but we have never looked back and are really grateful that we made this choice. We have experienced many benefits, including lower cost of living, sunnier weather, more access to nature, better shopping options, meeting new friends, and more. This is a great article that challenges all of us to take action instead of feeling like the world is against us.

Imagine my surprise, when scrolling down through the article to see my hometown of fort Madison, Iowa listed near the top of the affordable cities list! 15,000 people. I will say this, there is a reason why the cost is under $100 per square foot: Good paying jobs are scarce, amenities are non-existent, the schools are mediocre at best. Do yourself a favor, don’t save $50,000 on housing to sacrifice far more than that in future earnings. I can’t comment on overall life satisfaction, because, to each their own… It is a somewhat charming riverside city, but please, spend the money to live in a more desirable location. Strike a better balance.

Howdy fellow Iowan! Funny to read this as one of my friends just relocated to Fort Madison, IA because of the cheaper housing costs compared to the big city of Cedar Rapids :) where he was living. Of course Cedar Rapids, IA is still way way way cheaper than the East Coast where I moved from in 2015 for my own geographical arbitrage, in no small part because of this blog. But my friend found a good job before he moved to Fort Madison which is key, (he’s an electrician), even cheaper housing than Cedar, and so far is good with the move and likes Fort Madison – exactly your point about to each his own and it being a charming riverside city on the Mississippi.

Nice read. I myself have done pretty well with a couple of those strategies: first geoarbitrage in Japan (although I speak the language), then house hacking. We could live for roughly $2k/mo. living downtown in a 2nd-tier Japanese city (Sendai). Safe, convenient, great food. On house hacking, I studied up for years on real estate so I get how that may be daunting to some, but for us it’s turned into living for free for 2 years, then more recently choosing to pay half the mortgage to help out family. It takes work, but it will pay off if you put in the effort.

To those who still think house hacking is too hard, there’s a simple solution that’s old as dirt: Get a roommate. Get two even. If owning eventually is part of your dream, put whatever you save in housing expenses into a down payment savings account and pull the trigger once ready. After all, house hacking is basically just buying a house and then getting a roommate(s). If you’re reading this, MMM has already given you the tools; the only one capable of stopping you is yourself.

Lastly, on cheaper markets I’d find livable, on the East Coast I like Baltimore. You definitely have to be careful where you buy, but there’s opportunity for sure. Philly is another great place as mentioned above. I wouldn’t go anywhere near Cumberland (on MMM’s $200k list), but Pittsburgh might also be worth a look.

Good article! I would add to the suggestions to look for towns/cities that have Greyhound and related bus access and ideally also Amtrak right now. Additionally, use tools such as realtor.com to look at some of the major environmental risks (flood and fire) of any property being considered; having environmental risk integrated with real estate search engines is a relatively new feature, and unfortunately some of the best “deals” are squarely in the path of danger, from my experience. Finally, check relocation places out in person — ideally arriving without a car (such as by Amtrak or Greyhound) to see how it goes for you.

We have just sold our house near Austin, TX and moved our family of 5 to Lafayette, CO. Cost of living is significantly higher here and houses are incredibly expensive. My spouse is transgender and did not feel safe in TX anymore; We had to go. How strange to be political refugees. I never could have imagined us in this position. Due to housing prices in our new city, we have decided to become renters as we continue to pursue FI. Our equity money is going into the market. It feels very odd and countercultural to make this decision, but here we are. After decades of homeownership, have we gone backwards? Or will we be better off? Time will tell.

Mr. Money Mustache February 5, 2024, 2:35 pm

Welcome new neighbor! Maybe we’ll see you at one of our events at the MMMHQ Coworking space just up the road in Longmont this spring.

We probably should move, not because housing is unaffordable, in fact a massive home is $200k. Due to currency depreciation a home bought for $200k in 2010 is now only $80k. So housing is cheaper, but is a function of a dysfunctional economy.

However, many friends have moved to other countries because of a weak economy over past 2 decades. But to move it means we need to leave family behind, especially older parents. It is very hard to leave behind family connections, so we stay.

I guess you just have to be happy with your choices, because everything is a choice.

As others have said, the first half of this article (the FRED graph of average sales prices across the US) is statistically questionable and has the feel of “see? housing is actually affordable, you’re just wrong to be looking at actual sales prices in your area”. As you mention, it’s a national average, when all RE markets are local, so it’s unclear what it means at all. Another distortion is that the FRED data comes from FHA, which means that it excludes cash sales and sales with jumbo loans. This distortion tends to result in lower home prices than you see when looking at, say, the Case-Schiller data. Even if you average over the whole country.

But I’m glad I ground through that part because the rest of this has some really practical advice for how to find somewhere to live. There is a classic old Raptitude post “Most Lives are Lived by Default” which suggests that probably your current location is a side-effect of your job, or school, or relationship, and that you could do better if you actively tried to find the “right” location for you. Unfortunately the article provides no advice for _how_ to do this; it mostly suggests moving to a different neighborhood in your current town, with the assumption that you have a good idea of whether you want to be closer/further to nightlife or grocery stores or bike paths or whatever, and you just need to pull the trigger.

But for somebody who is near-FIRE, or “FIRE except for housing”, it’s hard to figure out where to even start. These resources are a great way to filter for locations that are financially reasonable and also in the right part of the country. Another thing I did was keep an eye on r/financialindependence and r/fatfire to see if anybody posted cool understated places to live. Chattanouga popped up, as did Kansas City MO, and Asheville NC.

In 2020 I visited a pile of such cities, as well as big ones like Philly and Portland and NYC, by going on AirBNB and finding a spare room that I could rent for a month or more. In the Portland area I wound up doing this for several months in a row, since it’s a huge place and you can change locations dramatically without leaving the metro area.

When I first started doing this I would always look to stay in whole houses, but this is the wrong approach! Aside from not distorting housing markets by using SFHs as hotels, you actually want to find a place with a host who you can talk to about the city and who can tell you about different neighborhoods. And if you rent spare rooms for long periods, it’s a surprisingly affordable thing to do. Especially as you can often meet people who are willing to let you stay with them without going through a fee-skimming platform like AirBNB.

This strategy might only be practical for single light-travelling digital nomad types but I encourage anybody to seriously consider it.

Thanks for the Albuquerque shoutout! It’s not a perfect place to live, but if you like being outside, it’s hard to do better for what it costs to live here.

FIRE is often about making different choices than everyone else to emphasize the things that really matter to you. You rent a small apartment close to work instead of buying a McMansion in the exurbs. You bike or walk instead of driving a 3-row SUV. You cook at home instead of eating out. You go to the library instead of the movie theater…

…and you move to New Mexico instead of Colorado.

If you’re still working, the national labs are solidly above-average employers that emphasize work-life balance. The outdoor recreation is almost as good as Colorado, and Durango is only a few hours away if you want bigger mountains. There’s a nice airport, a zoo, great museums, and 3 Costcos. The weather is great: cooler than Phoenix in the summer, warmer than Denver in the winter, and sunny almost all the time. Plus, the state is doing lots to support working families, with subsidized daycare and free college tuition.

So if you’re discouraged about how much it costs to live in Bend or Boulder, make less popular choice and check out New Mexico.

As a former Coloradoan, newly adopted New Mexican I can reiterate Joel’s statements. NM isn’t perfect but I feel like I have greater access to outdoor recreation here in NM than I did in the Front Range of Colorado, plus much less people to compete with. There are slightly more sunny days, so I can’t complain about that either.

I’m in Santa Fe, which is pretty comparable to many parts of Colorado regarding cost of living and the weather feels nearly identical to Colorado with our almost 7000′ elevation. Santa Fe punches above it’s weight as a city in regards to culture, restaurants, and museums. There is a good bit of tourism that feeds into that, but the restaurant scene is pretty great. The history of the region keeps me engaged as I continue to learn more about the area.

I keep eyeballing the affordability of Albuquerque and the offerings of a city that is 5x the size of Santa Fe, but Santa Fe fits the bill for now

The key thing, as this article exemplifies, is to EXAMINE both reality, and your own assumptions. So much “can’t afford a house” mania is based on vague unexamined feelings, and vague media-based proclamations. When you cut through that with a bunch of facts and self-examination . . . the world opens up. As this piece shows. In our case, a limiting factor (we thought) was the “must be close to family” idea. Then we realized that 1. family members keep making plans and moving without consulting us, so why base our whole lives on their (temporary) locations? 2. once we did the math and realized how often we “see family” it became clear that 3 visits a year with a couple of family events each time would cover all the hanging-out time we do, anyway. YMMV.

We love to see these people! But in reality, they’re all busy, they move around, and there’s a limit to everyone’s time. So now we are free to live mostly in Europe, where we prefer to be (and where it’s cheap to live a great, low-footprint life), and not feel disloyal because of some presumed idea of “being too far away from family.” We see them as much as ever did! Now it’s just during our annual out-and-back migration. So yeah: really, truly examine everything that seems to be liming your choices.

I think the one thing you missed calling out is how this is especially relevant to FIRE folks who are no longer working. Many of these lower cost cities don’t have the high paying jobs that really helps us along the way.

Personally I went the route of moving to a small apartment and renting in a HCOL city to maximize my income in my younger years. Now that I’m coming up on 40, I’ve moved to a small town in MN and enjoying the much lower cost of living.

The other cool aspect of this idea is that you can live in a very neat neighborhood within these type of towns. For example, I’m living in the heart of the historic neighborhood within walking distance of two lakes and downtown for super cheap. If I had done that in any moderate cost of living city, I’d pay 5-10x as much for housing. So while it’s a small town, it’s still very walkable & bikeable because I’m not stuck out in some suburban wasteland.

#8552. 4 High-Protein Dessert Recipes That Taste Good—and Will Help You Hit Your Macros

As we know, protein is a crucial part of healthy eating and building muscle. Without adequate daily protein, the chances of packing on all the muscle you want are slim.

While the ideal amount of protein will vary from individual to individual, it’s a good idea to spread out your intake of this crucial macro throughout the day to make it easier to get all that you need. Trying to pack 100 grams of protein into a single meal is never a wise move. Who ever said that getting your fill of protein needs to stop at dinner? The protein spread can (and should) include dessert. With a little effort and know-how, you can give your ab-friendly sweat treats a protein boost without making them taste all healthy and what-not. Using the right ingredients, it’s certainly possible to make a dessert that gives you 10 grams or more of protein, which is significant in your daily pursuit to get enough. And, sure, you could just blend together a post-dinner protein shake, but where’s the fun in that?

Higher-protein desserts, be it for an end-of-day treat or part of a game day spread, can help you reach your goals for this clutch macronutrient. Here’s how to make some treats that do much more than satisfy a sweet tooth. Everything in moderation, right?

Certain ingredients can give your treats a protein boost. So if you’re looking for a dessert that’ll help you build muscle, include any of these protein heroes.

Protein Powder: Good for much more than your post-gym recovery shakes, versatile protein powder can be used in a huge variety of dessert recipes, both cooked and uncooked. For baking, it can replace some of the flour in a recipe. But it’s best to use plant-based protein powders in baking recipes like muffins and cakes as they give a much better texture than powders made from whey.

Peanut Butter Powder: This is the best thing to add nutty taste to dessert that you probably aren’t using. Peanut butter powder is made by pressing roasted peanuts to remove most of their natural oils, then grinding the defatted peanuts into a fine powder. This process significantly reduces the fat and calorie content compared to peanut butter, and results in a more protein-dense product. A good buy is Naked Nutrition Peanut Butter Powder.

Greek Yogurt: Enhance the protein content of your desserts by using Greek yogurt or Skyr instead of regular yogurt in recipes. It’s an easy substitution that packs an extra protein punch with minimal change to the flavor or texture.

Chia Seeds: Chia seeds offer four grams of protein in just two tablespoons —and they help create a creamy pudding that will be a delicious high-protein dessert (or breakfast).

These (mostly) healthy high protein desserts are sure to satisfy and will help ramp up your protein intake throughout the day.

In a blender or food processor, blend together the cottage cheese, maple syrup and vanilla until smooth. Transfer to a mixing bowl and stir in the oat flour, peanut butter powder, and cocoa powder until well incorporated. Store in an airtight container in the refrigerator. It should stay fresh for up to one week.

This protein-heavy, sweet bread is great for breakfast, dessert, or a snack. Sweet potato provides natural sweetness, while peanut butter adds richness and some additional protein to each slice. It’s great with a generous smear of cream cheese. Be sure to use a plant-based protein powder instead of whey for better texture.

Preheat oven to 350°F. Line a standard-sized loaf pan with parchment paper or use a non-stick silicone loaf pan.

In a large bowl, mix together flour, protein powder, baking powder, baking soda, cinnamon, and salt. In a separate bowl, whisk together sweet potato, peanut butter, milk, maple syrup, and vanilla. Add wet ingredients to bowl with dry ingredients and mix gently until everything is moist. Pour batter into pan and smooth the surface with a spatula. Sprinkle on peanuts and press them down lightly to adhere.

Bake for 40 minutes, or until a toothpick inserted into the center of the loaf comes out mostly clean. Allow loaf to cool in pan for 10 minutes before cooling the loaf further on a metal rack.

Here’s how to give your dessert a taste of the tropics. The superpower of chia seeds is that they soak up liquid like a sponge, which produces a pudding-like texture. This is also a stand-out make-ahead breakfast option. Greek yogurt adds plenty of protein, but you can go bigger on this macro by also blending in your favorite protein powder.

Place mango, milk, yogurt, honey, lime juice, lime zest, ginger and a pinch of salt in a blender and blend until smooth. Divide among 2 jars. Add half of the chia seeds to each jar and stir to combine. Sprinkle on almonds or pistachios. Seal shut and chill for at least 3 hours and up to 3 days.

Avocado gives these ice cream-like frozen cups a fudgy consistency and plenty of good nutrition. Protein powder adds a solid amount of the muscle-making macro, bananas are here for some natural sweetness, and cayenne provides as surprising spicy kick. Only if all ice cream could be this good for you and still taste great.

Place bananas, avocado flesh, nut butter, protein powder, maple syrup or honey, cocoa powder, cinnamon, cayenne, and a pinch of salt in a blender or food processor container and process until smooth.

Line muffin pan with 8 paper liners. (You can skip this step if using silicone muffin cups). Scoop banana batter into muffin cups. Sprinkle on flaky salt if using. Place tray in the freezer and freeze for at least 2 hours, or until solid. Unmold fudge pucks and store in the freezer in an airtight container until ready to serve. When ready to serve, leave fudge pucks out at room temperature for a few minutes to soften slightly.

Building a company with a cofounder puts you through pressures nobody warns you about, plus the usual startup whiplash. Noah was our co-founder at Alertive Healthcare, our previous startup. He led product, engineering and design teams. He thinks like an engineer. The question he asks reframes the entire problem, and then he proceeds to build the answer.

Here’s the problem he found. Every physician in an ambulatory clinic runs against a clock, and the tell is the glancing. The wall clock. The watch. The timer in the screen’s corner. Patients catch every one of those looks, and they read them. Noah fixed it with an app, and he fixed it elegantly.

Article’s below. See whether his solution works for you. Full disclosure: Noah is a friend. I was paid no cash, no coins, no crypto and no farm eggs to write this. I just think he’s onto something.

I originally built Haptica Timer for my wife, who is a physician.

Like many clinicians, she spends much of her day moving from one patient visit to the next. She is constantly balancing two responsibilities that can sometimes feel at odds: being fully present with the patient in front of her while also staying aware of a demanding clinic schedule.

She did not want to keep looking at the wall clock. She did not want to glance at her phone or repeatedly raise her wrist during a conversation. Even when those actions are completely innocent, they can make a patient feel rushed or leave them wondering whether the physician is still listening.

What she needed was simple: a quiet way to understand how much time had passed without visibly checking the time.

That was the starting point for Haptica Timer.

The original idea was to create subtle vibration cues that could be felt on the wrist without interrupting a conversation. Just as importantly, the timer needed to repeat automatically.

A clinician should not have to remember to start another timer before every appointment or continually manage an app throughout the day.

Capital protection and double-digit monthly cash flow, without becoming a landlord.

Tue, Oct 13  ·  10:00 am PT  ·  11:00 am MT  ·  1:00 pm ET

Instead, the timing pattern could follow the natural rhythm of the clinic schedule, repeating from one visit to the next.

The goal was never to force every patient encounter into a rigid block of time. Some appointments need more time, and physicians must always be free to respond to what the patient needs.

The goal was simply to give clinicians a private sense of where they were in the visit, reduce the need to manually track time, and help the day move more smoothly without taking attention away from the patient.

The rest of this article is written by Jorge Sanchez, one of my former co-founders at Alertive Healthcare.

A patient is explaining something important.

The appointment may have started as a routine follow-up, but another concern has surfaced. It deserves attention. At the same time, the clinician knows the visit is beginning to run long and that another patient is waiting.

This is a normal part of medicine. Patient visits do not always follow a predictable path.

The challenge goes beyond simply keeping appointments short. It is remaining engaged with the person in front of you while still respecting the time of every patient who comes afterward.

Most clinicians develop their own ways of managing this. They glance at the clock, check the computer, look down at a watch, or try to estimate how much time has passed.

None of these approaches is necessarily wrong, but they’re all rather visible.

Patients may notice when attention shifts, particularly during emotional, personal, or complicated conversations. Even a quick glance can change the feeling in the room.

At the same time, losing awareness of time can affect the rest of the clinic day. A few additional minutes across several appointments can create longer waits, less time for documentation, hurried transitions, and increasing pressure on both clinicians and staff.

The problem is not the clock itself. The problem is needing to continually look for it.

A traditional timer is designed to capture your attention.

It makes a sound, displays a notification, lights up a screen, or requires you to look at it. Those features are useful in many settings, but they are not always appropriate during a medical visit.

An audible alarm would interrupt the conversation. A phone notification could feel out of place. A visible countdown could become another thing competing for the clinician’s attention.

The better solution was a less noticeable timer.

A subtle vibration could provide awareness without changing the conversation. The clinician could feel that a certain amount of time had passed and decide what, if anything, to do with that information.

That cue might prompt the clinician to summarize the discussion, confirm the care plan, address the patient’s final concern, or decide that the conversation needs to continue.

One of the most practical parts of Haptica is its ability to run repeating timers.

Clinic schedules often follow a regular cadence. Appointments may be scheduled in 15, 20, 30, or 40-minute blocks, sometimes with a short period between visits for documentation or transition.

Once the timing pattern is configured, the timer can repeat automatically.

This means the clinician does not need to start a new timer before every patient. There is no need to repeatedly open the app or remember to reset it as the day progresses.

For example, a physician might choose to receive one gentle cue when most of the visit has passed and another near the scheduled end. The timer can then pause briefly and begin the next cycle automatically for the following appointment.

This repeating pattern is important because it allows the timer to support the workflow without becoming another workflow to manage.

The experience is less like operating a stopwatch and more like maintaining a quiet awareness of the clinic’s rhythm.

A typical appointment may include reviewing concerns, gathering relevant history, performing an examination, discussing options, answering questions, agreeing on a plan, documenting the encounter, and preparing for the next patient.

When time awareness is lost early in the visit, the final portions can become compressed. The clinician may have less time to explain the plan, complete documentation, or transition thoughtfully to the next appointment.

A discreet timing cue can help the clinician recognize where they are in that process.

It may provide an opportunity to move from information gathering into decision-making, begin summarizing the plan, or identify a concern that deserves a separate follow-up rather than trying to address everything at once.

The repeating timer also reduces the small amount of mental and operational effort involved in managing separate timers throughout the day. Once configured, it can continue through the clinic schedule with minimal interaction.

During a routine follow-up, a subtle vibration lets the physician know that most of the scheduled time has passed.

Nothing interrupts the conversation. The patient does not hear or see anything.

The physician may begin bringing the visit together by reviewing the plan, confirming the next steps, and asking whether there is one final concern that needs to be addressed.

The cue does not end the visit. It helps the physician recognize that it may be time to transition naturally toward a conclusion.

During another visit, the vibration occurs while a patient is discussing something emotional or unexpected.

The physician feels the cue but chooses not to act on it.

The conversation continues because the patient needs more time.

This is an important part of how Haptica is intended to work. It provides awareness, and leaves the clinician to decide what the moment requires.

On a busy day, small delays can build quickly.

A few extra minutes across several morning appointments may become a significant delay by the afternoon. Patients wait longer, staff members work to catch up, documentation may accumulate, and the clinician may begin to feel increasingly rushed.

A repeating timer does not solve every scheduling or workflow challenge.

It can, however, provide a consistent sense of time throughout the day without requiring the clinician to repeatedly manage it.

That awareness may help identify when a visit is drifting, when it is time to begin summarizing, or when a concern may be better addressed through a separate follow-up.

Even when the physician decides to continue the visit, that decision is made with a clearer understanding of where the day stands.

Being present does not require completely losing awareness of time. In some cases, greater time awareness may make it easier to remain present.

When clinicians know where they are in a visit, they may feel less pressure to mentally track the clock. They can focus more fully on the patient and make a deliberate decision about whether to continue, transition, or arrange additional time.

The timer stays in the background. Clinical judgment remains at the center.

We did not want to create another complicated productivity system.

Clinicians already work with numerous systems, alerts, documentation requirements, and administrative tasks. Haptica was designed to address one specific problem without adding another layer of complexity.

It does not need to dominate the visit or become another screen to manage. The less attention it requires, the better it supports the reason it was created.

The purpose is to give clinicians one small, private signal that helps them use their time and judgment more intentionally.

According to the 2026 Medscape Physician Compensation Report, average physician pay reached $386,000 this year, up 3% from 2025 and enough to outpace the 2.7% core inflation rate.

Eight specialties crossed half a million dollars, led by orthopedic surgery at $611,000. 53% of physicians said they feel fairly compensated individually, the highest share in years. All wonderful news.

However, 61% of physicians still believe the profession as a whole is underpaid, and the average workweek barely budged. 63% of physicians blame bureaucratic work and electronic health records for their burnout. 14% of physicians say that they’re planning to leave clinical medicine altogether because of it.

And hospital systems aren’t going out of their way to ease the situation. Private equity and mergers bring in money that should help expand staff and provide a better work environment.

On the contrary, doctors face heavier workloads than ever with no room for PTO. All to protect the bottom line for those at the top.

Private health systems chasing profit and the policy turmoil of declining reimbursement and Medicaid funding work together to create the perfect storm of doctors at their wits’ end. This month we saw exactly how that plays out in real life.

Nearly 150 unionized doctors at two Twin Cities hospitals went on strike, in what’s believed to be the first walkout by private sector hospital doctors in U.S. history.

This was not a spur-of-the-moment decision, but came after three years of bargaining that went nowhere. The health system had made $6 billion in 2025 revenue but was negotiating pay and sick time as if there were nothing left to give.

The cherry on top? A $26 billion merger behind closed doors.

In case you missed it: The Great Debate of Physician Unionization

Doctors represented by Doctors Council SEIU picketed outside Allina Health’s Mercy Hospital in Coon Rapids and its Unity campus in Fridley for four days starting September 14, carrying signs reading “patients over profits.”

The union voted to unionize in 2023, sat through more than 60 bargaining sessions and authorized the strike with 90% support in July before giving the required 10 days’ notice.

Allina downplayed the disruption, stating that the union represents only about 10% of the physicians credentialed at both campuses and told the Minnesota Reformer that 37 union doctors crossed the picket line while 40 weren’t scheduled to work that week. Both campuses stayed open. The strike ran alongside a separate seven-day walkout by roughly 60 Allina hospice nurses.

Hospitalist Dr. Amber Galarowicz, on the union’s bargaining team, said that the fight isn’t just about pay. “We need to be able to stand up for ourselves,” she said.

Paid sick leave was likely the biggest factor. Minnesota law entitles full-time workers to six days a year but the doctors say they can’t take paid time off when they’re sick without dipping into vacation days.

Allina says its physicians already have paid leave and that it’s in compliance with state law. Never mind the fact that healthcare workers face a higher risk of getting ill.

“It’s become unsustainable for us to continue working like that,” said Dr. Alia Sharif, another bargaining team hospitalist.

Dr. John Wurst, who was part of the strike, said that doctors are also fighting to keep decision-making in physician hands, pointing to artificial intelligence tools that now weigh in on insurance billing as one example of ground already lost.

“We feel like we’re being excluded from decisions that affect the care of our patients,” Wurst said, adding that leaving physicians out of those calls means medical resources won’t end up allocated in a way that actually serves the community.

Cost of living adjustments have been part of the back and forth since last fall. This is amid rising inflation and fuel costs.

Coverage itself is also disputed. Because doctors often work across multiple Allina facilities, the two sides can’t agree on which physicians the union contract actually covers.

Doctors need to spend at least 20% of their time at Unity or Mercy to qualify for the bargaining unit but how that 20% gets calculated is still up in the air.

Apart from this local dispute, doctors across the nation are contending with policy changes that directly affects how much they earn.

Medicare’s 2026 physician fee schedule finalized a 2.5% “efficiency adjustment” that CMS says reflects services becoming easier to perform over time.

The policy applies to roughly 7,700 billing codes, including surgical procedures, diagnostic imaging interpretation, outpatient interventions, interventional pain management and orthopedic services.

Learn more: A Physician’s Guide to Medicare’s Specialty Care Changes — What’s Really Happening?

By law, Medicare physician payments have to stay budget neutral, meaning a raise for one group of doctors requires a cut somewhere else. Primary care physicians and time-based services keep the 2.5% increase Congress passed last year.

Specialists performing procedures have to watch that same increase get wiped out by the efficiency adjustment, and in some cases end up with a net cut once other changes are factored in.

The American Medical Association says that these changes will affect certain specialties more than others. More than a third of oncologists face cuts as steep as 20%. Over half of internists can expect reductions of 5% or more, and the same goes for 80% of infectious disease physicians.

One physician commented that as one of two infectious disease specialists in her region, the cuts would force her to refuse care to Medicare and Medicaid patients or simply retire.

The Congressional Budget Office estimates that the 2025 reconciliation law will cut federal Medicaid spending by $911 billion over 10 years, and 16 million people are projected to lose coverage through Medicaid or the ACA marketplace.

The layoffs stemming from these policy changes are no longer hypothetical. Back in June, Hennepin Healthcare in Minneapolis, in the same metro area as Allina’s Mercy and Unity campuses, announced roughly 100 layoffs this year and cut 100 inpatient beds, citing a $50 million shortfall tied directly to Medicaid revenue losses.

Trinity Health said it expects to lose $1.5 billion to “recent and future government policy changes.” Baptist Health in Arkansas laid off 150 employees, including 10 physicians, while shutting down its nephrology, pulmonary, oncology and infectious disease services.

Allina itself is telling employees that its economic decisions stem from “rising costs for drugs, supplies and labor, ongoing reimbursement pressures, increases in claim denials from insurance companies, and anticipated impacts from federal policy and reimbursement changes.”

Also read: What Physicians Should Know About the CMS Cut That Shaves Your Same-Day E/M Payment in Half

On top of all this is Allina’s proposed merger with Sutter Health, a California nonprofit, that would combine the two systems into a $26 billion operation spanning 39 hospitals across three states.

The merger is under review by the Minnesota Attorney General’s Office and opposed by labor unions who warn that consolidation tends to raise costs for patients while suppressing wage growth for the workers providing care.

Sharif said she doesn’t expect the union to block the deal but she’d like a community benefits agreement that shields against layoffs and service cuts, similar to one recently reached between the state and Sanford Health over its acquisition of a Robbinsdale hospital.

Capital protection and double-digit monthly cash flow, without becoming a landlord.

Tue, Oct 13  ·  10:00 am PT  ·  11:00 am MT  ·  1:00 pm ET

For those who aren’t working at Mercy or Unity, this may feel abstract. It’s not.

Physician unionization has been on the rise because things that used to work, like individual negotiation, specialty societies lobbying CMS, and professional goodwill, keep losing to system-level budget decisions.

If you’re an employed physician, this deserves your attention. The same reimbursement structure and Medicaid cuts may come for whatever health system signs your paycheck.

Strikes make headlines because everyone has an opinion on them. Bureaucrats like to dismiss legitimate physician demands as unreasonable. But the jig is up, and the people are decrying the monopolization of our healthcare system.

The question is, what will it take to stop the consolidation machine?

Insights on building wealth, making informed career decisions, and achieving financial independence from a fellow physician.

Physician on FIRE and The Prudent Plastic Surgeon share a mission to help physicians build financial knowledge, independence, and control over their future.

Dr. Jordan Frey is a full-time practicing plastic surgeon and founder of The Prudent Plastic Surgeon, read by 20,000+ physicians. For five years, he has shared insights on personal finance, investing, career decisions, and financial independence while continuing to practice medicine.

A Physician on FIRE Partnership As part of our partnership, Physician on FIRE periodically shares select articles from The Prudent Plastic Surgeon with its readers.

About three months ago, I decided to actually give physician expert witness work a shot.

It was something that had been on my radar for a while. I knew other physicians did it. I knew it could be a lucrative side gig. And, at least on paper, it seemed to check a lot of the boxes that I look for in a physician side gig.

And three months later, after a bunch of cold outreach, a lot of conversations, a course on expert witness work, and several actual cases, including one involving a zebra, I figured it was a good time to share what I’ve learned so far.

The first thing I learned is that getting started in expert witness work is not particularly exciting.

Learn what Class A, B, and C really mean, how building quality affects distributions and resale, and why some passive investors prefer properties outside the top tier.

There was no moment where I signed up somewhere and cases suddenly started pouring in. Instead, there were a lot of emails, Zoom calls, and phone calls.

I reached out to lawyers. I talked to physicians who were already doing expert witness work. Plus I joined physician expert witness networks. I introduced myself, explained my expertise as a reconstructive plastic surgeon, sent my CV, and basically said, “If you ever need someone like me, keep me in mind.”

And I’ll admit, this felt a little uncomfortable. We aren’t really trained to market ourselves. For me, there was definitely a little bit of a feeling that I was shamelessly promoting myself. But eventually I started thinking about it differently.

We really are experts in our fields. And there are legal cases where an objective medical opinion can legitimately help a patient, a physician, or both. My job isn’t to advocate for whichever attorney happens to hire me. It’s to review the information and give an honest opinion based on my training and experience.

Once I reframed it that way, the outreach became a lot easier.

At the same time, I quickly realized that being an expert physician doesn’t automatically make you an expert witness. I understood the broad strokes. Review the medical records. Understand what happened. Form an opinion. Explain it.

But I didn’t really know how to structure a case review, what attorneys were looking for, how to write a report, how to create a fee schedule, or even how the business side of expert witness work typically operates.

That’s when I took Amy Fogelman’s High Rock Academy expert witness course. I found it incredibly helpful, particularly because it wasn’t just theoretical. There were actual resources and templates that I could use when cases started coming in, including report templates that I ultimately used for my first cases.

That preparation ended up being pretty well timed.

About six weeks after I really started pursuing this, I got my first case.

Ironically, my first case didn’t come from any of the cold outreach I had been doing. It came from a local physician friend who knew an attorney looking for someone with my expertise.

There’s probably an important lesson in there. You can send emails and join directories and market yourself all you want, but relationships still matter. The case involved aesthetic breast surgery and, to this point, has also been my most extensive case. There were a lot of records. There were depositions. And there were hours spent reviewing everything and figuring out exactly what happened.

Then I got on the phone with the attorneys.

This was probably the first time the work really clicked for me. They had very specific questions, and my job was essentially to do something that I already do every day as a physician: take a lot of complicated medical information, figure out what actually matters, form an opinion, and explain that opinion clearly.

That case is actually still ongoing, so there may be more work to come.

But after that first case, others started showing up.

I’ve now reviewed a handful of cases. Some have been relatively run-of-the-mill. And then there was the case involving an injury from a zebra.

I don’t remember that particular scenario coming up during plastic surgery residency.

But even that case reinforced what I’ve come to think is the biggest advantage of expert witness work for physicians: we already know how to do most of this. We spend our careers reviewing information, identifying what is relevant, synthesizing it, forming an assessment, and communicating that assessment to someone else. Sometimes that someone is a patient. Sometimes it’s another physician. And sometimes it’s an insurance company or hospital administrator.

In expert witness work, it happens to be an attorney.

That’s why, after only three months, I think this may be one of the better physician side gigs available. I used to list expert witness work as something I hadn’t personally done yet. Now I can at least start filling in that blank from experience.

Obviously, the income is part of the appeal.

One of the harder things when I started was figuring out what to charge. Talking to physicians who had done this before helped, as did seeing how others structured their fees.

I ultimately landed at $750 per hour with a five-hour minimum retainer.

So when I’m retained, I receive payment upfront for those first five hours. If the work goes beyond that, I bill additional time. I’ve had cases that exceeded the retainer and others that didn’t. But what matters to me isn’t just the hourly rate.

I’ve reviewed records early in the morning before my kids wake up. I’ve done work during their practices. And I’ve worked on cases in between operations while waiting for turnover.

That’s a meaningful distinction from clinical medicine, where income is about as directly tied to our physical presence as you can get. If I’m operating, seeing patients, or taking call, I can make money. If I’m not there, I generally don’t.

Expert witness work is still active income. I’m certainly not going to put it in the same category as the passive income streams I’ve built. But it’s active income on my terms.

Not every potential case turns into actual work.

This is particularly true with expert witness directories and referral companies. You may get contacted about a case, review some preliminary information, give a brief response, and then never hear anything else because the attorney chose someone else.

Do that enough times and it can become a real time suck. That’s one reason why, so far, I’ve preferred building direct relationships with attorneys.

And once you do get a case, my early impression is that the best marketing strategy is probably incredibly simple: Do a good job.

Be responsive. Be timely. You also need to be thorough without writing a 47-page treatise when three pages will do. Answer the questions being asked. Be easy to work with.

And most importantly, be honest. If your opinion isn’t what the attorney wants to hear, that’s still your opinion. The entire value of being an expert witness comes from being objective.

Do those things consistently and, I suspect, repeat business and referrals will follow.

There is one major part of expert witness work that I still haven’t experienced: Testifying.

I haven’t been deposed or testified at trial yet. So that’s an obvious blind spot in everything I’m saying here.

From talking to more experienced physician experts, my understanding is that most cases don’t ultimately involve courtroom testimony. A lot of the work is record review, conversations with attorneys, and written reports. Still, testimony is different. Being questioned by an opposing attorney while defending your opinions is not something we routinely do in clinical medicine.

When I eventually have that experience, I’ll write about it.

Physician expert witness work isn’t passive income. It’s scalable but requires effort, much in the same way that other physician side income streams can potentially require. And it isn’t something where you send a few emails and immediately have an overflowing pipeline of cases.

Capital protection and double-digit monthly cash flow, without becoming a landlord.

Tue, Oct 13  ·  10:00 am PT  ·  11:00 am MT  ·  1:00 pm ET

But it does something that I think is incredibly valuable for physicians.

It takes expertise that we already spent years, really decades, developing and gives us another way to use it. And unexpectedly, I think it has already made me a better physician.

Reading cases retrospectively makes you think differently about documentation. It makes you think about how clinical decisions will look when someone reviews the chart a year later without any of the context you had in the moment. I’ve already found myself bringing some of those lessons back into my own practice.

A handful of hours of expert witness work can generate income comparable to working an extra clinical shift. Except I can do those hours before my kids wake up, at a practice, or whenever else they fit into my life.

And that gets back to the whole reason I’m pursuing financial freedom as a physician in the first place.

The goal isn’t just more money. It’s more control over my time. Three months in, expert witness work seems like a pretty good way to create a little more of both.

The ultimate domestic travel rewards benefit for families and couples

Imagine this: you book a flight for yourself, and your spouse — or your best friend, or your mom — flies with you for the cost of taxes alone. Not a discount. Not a sale. Completely. Free. For up to two full calendar years. That's the Southwest Companion Pass, and it is, without question, the single most powerful perk in all of domestic travel rewards. The ChooseFI community has a saying: if you only ever pursue one travel rewards strategy in your life, make it this one. Here's the math that makes your jaw drop. A round-trip Southwest flight from Denver to Cancún might run $400 per person. A family of four flying during spring break? You're looking at $1,600 cash. But with the Companion Pass, you pay for two tickets and the other two fly free — cutting your out-of-pocket cost in half, every single flight, for nearly two years. Run the numbers over a year of typical family travel and you're looking at **$2,000 to $8,000 in total value** from a single benefit. The CPP (cents per point) range here — **1.5 to 5.9 cents per point** — is what makes this genuinely remarkable. Southwest's Rapid Rewards program values points at roughly 1.4 cents toward any flight. But the Companion Pass doesn't just redeem points efficiently; it *doubles the value of every redemption you make while it's active*. That's the pricing inefficiency the loyalty system has quietly built in, and the FI community is uniquely positioned to exploit it. Think about what 135,000 points normally buys: roughly $1,890 worth of Southwest flights. Solid, but not earth-shattering. Now attach the Companion Pass, and those same points — redeemed strategically over two years — effectively unlock $3,780 or more in flight value for your household. No blackout dates. No seat restrictions. No change fees. Just book, fly, repeat. This isn't a first-class lounge or a lie-flat bed over the Pacific. It's something arguably more valuable for the FI-minded family: **sustainable, repeatable, nearly free domestic travel** that works with your actual life.

The Companion Pass isn't a points redemption — it's a status benefit. That distinction is everything, and it's the insight that separates people who get this from people who miss it entirely.

Here's how it works: Southwest grants the Companion Pass when you earn 135,000 qualifying Rapid Rewards points in a single calendar year. Once you hit that threshold, you designate one person as your companion, and that person flies with you on every flight — paid or points — for the remainder of that calendar year plus the entire following calendar year.

The key word is "earn." Points transferred in from partners count. Credit card signup bonuses count. Shopping portal purchases count. Almost every way you accumulate points counts toward the 135,000 threshold — except points purchased directly from Southwest.

The pricing inefficiency here is a calendar arbitrage opportunity. If you earn the Companion Pass on January 2nd, you get it for the rest of that year and all of the next year — nearly two full calendar years of 2-for-1 flights. If you earn it on November 15th, you get roughly 13 months. The strategy is to time your credit card signup bonuses to post in January, maximizing your benefit window.

Most ChooseFI members build their 135,000 points through a combination of strategies:

Chase Ultimate Rewards → Southwest Rapid Rewards (1:1, Instant) Chase transfers to Southwest at a 1:1 ratio and the transfer is instant — points appear in your Rapid Rewards account within minutes. This makes Chase points (earned on cards like the Chase Sapphire Preferred or Ink Business cards) the most efficient fuel for this strategy.

Marriott Bonvoy → Southwest Rapid Rewards (3:1, 1-5 days) Marriott transfers at a 3:1 ratio (3 Marriott points = 1 Southwest point), and transfers take 1-5 days. This is a less efficient path — use it only if you have a surplus of Marriott points and no better option.

The most reliable path to 135,000 points is stacking Southwest credit card signup bonuses. Southwest's consumer and business cards frequently offer bonuses of 50,000-75,000 points each. A couple who each opens one card, or one person who opens both a personal and business card, can often hit the threshold with signup bonuses alone — before spending a dollar on the portal.

Since Southwest charges no fuel surcharges on award flights and points never expire, there's no penalty for building this balance over several months. The Rapid Rewards program is revenue-based with dynamic pricing, meaning points cover the full fare including taxes — no hidden redemption fees to erode your value.

Log into your Chase Ultimate Rewards account and your Southwest Rapid Rewards account and tally your existing points. You need 135,000 qualifying Rapid Rewards points earned in a single calendar year to trigger the Companion Pass. Note: points already sitting in your Rapid Rewards account from prior years don't count — you need to earn 135,000 in the target calendar year.

The optimal window is October through December of the prior year. Apply for Southwest credit cards (personal and/or business) so that your signup bonuses post to your Rapid Rewards account in January. Verify with Southwest's current card offers — signup bonuses of 50,000-75,000 points are common. A couple can each apply for a card; a solo pursuer can apply for both a personal and a business card if they have qualifying self-employment income.

Call Chase or Southwest after your first statement closes to confirm when points will post. Timing is everything.

Once your signup bonuses post, calculate how many points you still need. If you're short:

Southwest will notify you by email once you've crossed 135,000 qualifying points. Log into your Rapid Rewards account at southwest.com and navigate to "My Account" → "Companion Pass" to confirm the benefit is active.

You can designate — and change — your companion up to three times per calendar year. Name your most frequent travel partner first. Go to southwest.com, log in, and find the Companion Pass section to add their name and contact information.

Searching is simple: go to southwest.com and search any route. Toggle between "$ Dollars" and "Rapid Rewards Points" to see your cost. When you book with points and your companion is designated, Southwest will automatically prompt you to add your companion to the same flight. Your companion pays taxes only — typically $5.60 each way for domestic flights.

Pro tip: Southwest opens its booking window 330 days in advance. For peak travel like spring break or holiday weeks, set a calendar reminder and book the day the window opens.

The Companion Pass works because Southwest treats it as a status benefit rather than a points redemption. Most airline companion programs require you to burn miles for the second ticket or limit usage to specific fare classes. Southwest flips this model: once you earn the pass, your companion flies on every single flight you take — paid or award — for the remainder of the qualifying year plus the entire following calendar year. The only cost is taxes. Because Southwest has no blackout dates, no fuel surcharges, and no change fees, the pass amplifies in value with every trip you take. The January-earning calendar arbitrage is the key optimization that turns a good benefit into an extraordinary one.

Let's make this real. It's March, and your family of four wants to spend a week in Orlando this July — theme parks, pool time, the works.

A quick search on southwest.com shows round-trip flights from Chicago Midway to Orlando for $320 per person. For four tickets, that's $1,280 cash. Standard family travel math: painful but doable.

You have the Companion Pass active, earned back in January. You book two tickets: yours at 22,000 Rapid Rewards points (worth ~$308 at 1.4 cents per point), and your spouse's ticket at $5.60 in taxes as your designated companion. Your two kids? You use 44,000 more points for their tickets. Total out-of-pocket: 66,000 points + $11.20 in taxes.

Let's value those 66,000 points at their Chase transfer cost — you transferred them 1:1 from Chase Ultimate Rewards, where they were worth roughly $825 in travel via the portal. But by pairing them with the Companion Pass, your spouse flies free, effectively doubling your points' purchasing power on this trip.

Cash price: $1,280. Your cost: 66,000 points + $11.20. That's a CPP of roughly 1.9 cents per point on the base redemption — but accounting for your companion flying free, the effective CPP on the entire trip rockets to 3.8 cents per point. Well within the 1.5–5.9 cent range where this sweet spot lives.

And here's what makes Southwest specifically wonderful for families: no change fees. Book in March, change in June when your kid's baseball tournament schedule shifts, rebook without penalty. No one in the FI community is paying $200-per-person change fees.

The experience itself? Economy class on Southwest, open seating, snacks, and friendly crew. It's not lie-flat business class to Tokyo — but that's not the point. The point is your family of four flies to Florida for a week, and the flights barely register on your annual budget. That's FI-level travel.

Time your credit card applications so signup bonuses post in January of your target year. A bonus that posts January 5th gives you until December 31st of the following year to use the Companion Pass — nearly 24 months of 2-for-1 flights. This single timing decision can mean the difference between 13 months and 23 months of value.

The Rapid Rewards Shopping Portal (rapidrewardsshopping.com) awards points on purchases at hundreds of retailers. Even after you've earned the Companion Pass, continuing to earn Rapid Rewards points means more flights at lower point costs. Treat it like a cashback portal and check it before any online purchase.

Southwest opens availability 330 days in advance. For Thanksgiving, Christmas, spring break, and summer weekends in popular markets, set a calendar reminder and book the exact morning the window opens. Southwest doesn't have blackout dates, but high-demand flights sell out in Wanna Get Away fare class — the cheapest points tier — quickly.

You can change your designated companion up to three times per calendar year. If your life situation changes — a different travel partner, a new relationship, a child aging into a separate ticket — use this flexibility. Just don't burn all three changes frivolously.

Purchased points do not count toward the 135,000 qualifying threshold for the Companion Pass. Don't make this mistake when you're close to the threshold — transfer from Chase instead.

Some people try to earn the Companion Pass in November or December. You'll get it for only a few weeks before the calendar resets. The math simply doesn't work. January earning is the only strategy worth pursuing.

The Southwest Rapid Rewards Performance Business Credit Card (or similar business cards) have separate signup bonuses that stack with personal card bonuses. If you have any self-employment income — freelancing, a side hustle, a rental property — you likely qualify. This is often the fastest path to 135,000 points for a single applicant.

Free calculators, a personalized FI roadmap, and a community of 25K+ on the same journey.

The Southwest Companion Pass was practically invented for the FI-minded family. If you have a consistent travel partner — a spouse, a partner, a parent you visit annually — and you fly domestically more than two or three times a year, this benefit will transform your travel budget.

Minimum points to get started: You need to earn 135,000 qualifying Rapid Rewards points in a single calendar year. In practice, this means you either need access to Southwest credit card signup bonuses (which requires good to excellent credit, typically 700+) or a substantial existing balance of Chase Ultimate Rewards points to transfer at 1:1.

How it fits the FI strategy: The Companion Pass is a force multiplier. Every dollar you would have spent on a second ticket stays in your investment accounts instead. Over a two-year Companion Pass window, a couple who takes six domestic trips per year could easily bank $2,000-$4,000 in travel savings — real money that compounds.

Who this is NOT for: Solo travelers get zero benefit from the Companion Pass. International travelers who primarily fly non-Southwest routes won't find much use here. And if you're averse to economy class or require a specific airline's premium cabin, this redemption isn't your path.

The Southwest Companion Pass earns a **moderate difficulty rating** — and that rating is almost entirely about the *earning*, not the booking. Once you have the Companion Pass, booking is literally the simplest award experience in travel rewards: search southwest.com, find your flight, click "Add Companion." There are no partner airlines to navigate, no availability calendars to decode, no call centers to endure. It's a 5/5 on ease of booking for a reason. The moderate rating comes from **three earning challenges**: **1. The credit requirement.** Southwest credit cards require good to excellent credit. If you're early in your credit-building journey, this strategy may need to wait 12-18 months while you strengthen your profile. **2. The timing discipline.** Earning the pass is straightforward, but earning it in January takes planning. You need to apply for cards 2-3 months in advance and coordinate signup bonus posting dates — something most people have never had to think about. **3. The 135,000-point threshold.** This is a real number. It requires intentional credit card strategy, not casual spending. For a single applicant without a business card, it may require supplementing with Chase transfers or portal activity. **How to overcome these challenges:** - Start planning in **October or November** for a January earn target - Check whether you qualify for a Southwest business card — it dramatically simplifies reaching the threshold - Use the Rapid Rewards Shopping Portal year-round to passively accumulate qualifying points If you've successfully applied for a travel rewards credit card before and you have a consistent travel partner, you can absolutely do this. The ChooseFI community has helped hundreds of families earn the Companion Pass — and not one of them regretted the effort.

Open a personal and/or business Southwest credit card so that signup bonuses of 50,000 to 75,000 points each will post to your Rapid Rewards account in January. Call to confirm when points will post after your first statement closes.

Once signup bonuses post, calculate your gap. Transfer Chase Ultimate Rewards at 1:1 (instant) to fill any shortfall. Use the Rapid Rewards Shopping Portal for additional earning on everyday purchases.

After Southwest confirms your Companion Pass, log in to southwest.com and designate your travel partner. Book flights as normal — Southwest will prompt you to add your companion for taxes only ($5.60 each way domestic).

Set calendar reminders for Thanksgiving, Christmas, spring break, and summer travel. Southwest opens its booking window 330 days in advance. Book the morning the window opens to lock in Wanna Get Away fares at the lowest point costs.

The Companion Pass is valid for the remainder of the calendar year in which you earn it plus the entire following calendar year. If you earn it on January 2nd, you get nearly 24 months of 2-for-1 flights. If you earn it in November, you get roughly 14 months. This is why timing your earning to January is the critical optimization.

Yes. Signup bonuses, spending on Southwest cards, points transferred from Chase Ultimate Rewards, and points earned through the Rapid Rewards Shopping Portal all count as qualifying points. The only points that do not count are those purchased directly from Southwest.

Yes. The Companion Pass works on both cash-purchased flights and flights booked with Rapid Rewards points. Your companion pays only taxes — typically $5.60 each way for domestic flights — regardless of how you booked the ticket.

Southwest allows you to change your designated companion up to three times per calendar year. Log into your Rapid Rewards account on southwest.com and update the companion information in the Companion Pass section. Plan strategically since you only get three changes per year.

The Southwest Companion Pass is the single most powerful domestic travel rewards benefit available to FI-minded families and couples. At a cost of 135,000 qualifying points — achievable through credit card signup bonuses and Chase transfers — you unlock nearly two full years of 2-for-1 flights on every Southwest route with no blackout dates and no change fees. A family of four taking six domestic trips per year can realistically save $2,000 to $4,000 annually, money that goes straight back into your investment accounts. Time your earning to January, stack your signup bonuses, and designate your most frequent travel partner. This is the redemption that makes domestic travel a rounding error in your FI budget.
